newsitem.title: USA: First Union says can look at buyback in '97.
newsitem.headline: First Union says can look at buyback in '97.

text.p: First Union Corp's pending acquisition of Keystone Investments Inc prevents the bank from doing share repurchases at this time, but the restriction will end during 1997, First Union Chairman and Chief Executive Edward Crutchfield said on Friday.

In response to a question during a conference call with reporters, he said Securities and Exchange Commission curbs that apply after a pooling-of-interests acquisition do not prevent First Union "from looking at (stock buybacks) in 1997."
Crutchfield also said that among acquisition possibilities for First Union, buying a big, out-of-market bank was the lowest priority.

He said the "most favored" type of acquisition would be one similar to the Keystone buy. Next would be "fill-in" acquisitions in markets where the company alredy operates, and a distant third would be a big, out-of-market deal, he said.
Crutchfield and other First Union executives spoke to reporters following a separate session with Wall Street analysts. Both events were preceded by announcement of higher internal performance goals.
Crutchfield said that in 10 years First Union has evolved from a "relatively small, one-bank operation" headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., into a 12-state bank operating from Florida to Connecticut.
The company grew through dozens of acquisitions, culminating in the purchase of First Fidelity Bancorp on January 1, 1996.

Tony Terracciano, former head of New Jersey-based First Fidelity and now president of First Union, said the northeast U.S. presents opportunities for "fill-in" deals, with acquisition candidates in the $2 billion asset range.

In response to a question, Terracciano said there was a "very strong burden of proof" against First Union entering New York City proper. First Union, following the First Fidelity deal, surrounds New York City with branches in New Jersey and Connecticut.

Crutchfield and other executives said the company's higher performance targets, including a return on common equity in the 18-20 percent range, compared to a prior target of 16-17 percent, depend on rapid growth in the capital management and capital markets areas, which are expected to grow much faster than the basic banking business.

Don McMullen, head of First Union's capital management area, said the goal in that business was to boost assets under management to $100 billion. With the Keystone deal, assets under management will total about $27.5 billion.
McMullen said getting to $100 billion would mean one or two mid-sized acquisitions.
Crutchfield said the banking business is presently about 80 percent traditional banking and 20 percent "Merrill Lynch-type" businesses such as capital markets and investment management.
He said the aim is to achieve higher growth and to shift the ratio to 60 percent traditional banking and 40 percent non-traditional.

In response to a question, Vice Chairman John Georgius confirmed that during the summer First Union looked into the possibility of selling about $1 billion in underperforming credit card receivables. He said the bank dropped the plan when it could not get the price it wanted.
He said the receivables in question are now part of a total portfolio of about $6 billion with a loss ratio of 6.0-6.5 percent.
First Union shares were off 7/8 to 71-7/8 in afternoon trading.
